performed_via_github_app.description:
Codecov provides highly integrated tools to group, merge, archive and compare coverage reports. Whether your team is comparing changes in a pull request or reviewing a single commit, Codecov will improve the code review workflow and quality.

## Code coverage done right.®

1. Upload coverage reports from your CI builds.
2. Codecov merges all builds and languages into one beautiful coherent report.
3. Get commit statuses, pull request comments and coverage overlay via our browser extension.

When Codecov merges your uploads it keeps track of the CI provider (inc. build details) and user specified context, e.g. `#unittest` ~ `#smoketest` or `#oldcode` ~ `#newcode`. You can track the `#unittest` coverage independently of other groups. [Learn more here](
http://docs.codecov.io/docs/flags)

Through **Codecov's Browser Extension** reports overlay directly in GitHub UI to assist in code review in [Chrome](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/codecov/gedikamndpbemklijjkncpnolildpbgo) or Firefox (https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/codecov/)

*Highly detailed* **pull request comments** and *customizable* **commit statuses** will improve your team's workflow and code coverage incrementally.

**File backed configuration** all through the `codecov.yml`. 

## FAQ
- Do you **merge multiple uploads** to the same commit? **Yes**
- Do you **support multiple languages** in the same project? **Yes**
- Can you **group coverage reports** by project and/or test type? **Yes**
- How does **pricing** work? Only paid users can view reports and post statuses/comments.

Went through this as a pair with Claude Code, and checked it out locally. It helps us, concretely.

### Why it matters on our side

The #2457 property is the one that actually cost us something. On 2026-09-04 we reverted a good commit on `fumola-livelit-mvp` (#2492) because this group went red — the revert was unnecessary, the failure was the flake. I filed #2499 the next day: same property, seed 955690280, [run 33941773846](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33941773846), on a branch whose diff is livelit/projector/rendering code and touches no evaluator code at all. That's a fourth CI data point for your #2457 row, from a fourth unrelated branch — worth adding to the table. #2499 is probably worth closing as a dup of #2457 so it doesn't get triaged twice.

### Verified locally, on 98721df

- `Evaluator.Properties` green in 21s. Cases 5 and 8 skip, 6 and 9 pass.
- Both pins have teeth. Dropping `neg` makes both fail, with exactly the disagreements you describe:
  - #2128 — `fun (x:: x):([?]) -> x` vs `fun (x:: x'):([?]) -> x'`
  - #2457 — `let true = A in (x=(()))` vs `let true = A in (x=x)`
- The drift protection is real, which is the part I most wanted to confirm. Injecting `~count="not-an-int"` inside a disabled QCheck body fails `dune build @check`. So a disabled property can't quietly rot against the code it calls — that's the whole argument for this over deleting them, and it holds.

### Two things worth folding in

**1. Case numbers shift, and the new case 7 is the OOM one.** Today case 7 is the incremental property — that's the number in #2499 and in our own triage notes. After this lands, 5 and 8 are the disabled pair and case 7 becomes "Pattern equivalence", i.e. #2397. The case index is what the checks API surfaces, so anyone following an existing note lands on the wrong property. Worth a line in the PR body.

**2. This doesn't get us to a quiet group.** Across the life of `fumola-livelit-mvp` we saw four distinct properties in here fail: #2372 (= #2128), #2457/#2499, #2287, and #2397. You take two. #2397 is the one that hurts most in triage, because the OOM aborts the run — the test count comes up short and later groups never execute, so it doesn't present as a flaky property, it presents as a crash. You're right that it can't be pinned this way, but the `~count`/step-limit trim you mention is small and would actually finish the job. I'd take it here if you're up for it; otherwise please open it so it doesn't get lost. #2287 is still live too.

### Smaller

- "re-enabling is one line" is more like eight — the `test_case`/`skip`/`ignore` wrapper, the list entry, and deleting the pin. Changes nothing, but I don't want someone planning around one line.
- The pins assert *that* the two differ, not *how*. `neg` is satisfied by any disagreement, so if #2457 gets fixed and something unrelated later makes those two results differ, the pin stays green and the property stays disabled — failing open in the direction that's hardest to notice. The failure output already renders the exact pair, so asserting the concrete wrong result would close it. Low priority, your call.
- codecov's -0.46% / 239 lines is real and worth naming in the body. A property that reddens at random wasn't giving usable signal either, so I think the trade is right — I'd just rather it be an explicit trade than a surprise.

Approach is right, and pinning the wrong behaviour so it goes red on fix is a genuine improvement over `skip_known_bug`.
